1	% Requires preamble: \usepackage{amsthm,amsmath,amssymb}
2	% and: \newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}
3	%      \newtheorem{corollary}[theorem]{Corollary}
4	%      \newtheorem{proposition}[theorem]{Proposition}
5	
6	\section{Bias Decomposition: When Debiasing Hurts}
7	\label{sec:theory}
8	
9	We formalize the bias that global misclassification correction introduces when subgroup error rates are heterogeneous.
10	Consider estimating the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) $\tau(z) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid Z = z]$, where $Z \in \{0, 1\}$ is a binary effect modifier observed only through a noisy annotation $\hat{Z}$.
11	The population consists of $K$ subgroups $S \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ with weights $w_s = P(S{=}s)$, each characterized by a $2 \times 2$ confusion matrix $C_s$ with symmetric error rate $\pi_s = P(\hat{Z} \neq Z \mid S{=}s)$.
12	Standard practice estimates a single confusion matrix $\bar{C} = \sum_s w_s C_s$ from expert annotations and applies its inverse uniformly to all observations, with pooled error rate $\bar{\pi} = \sum_s w_s \pi_s$.
13	We show that when error rates vary across subgroups, this global procedure introduces a bias with an exact product form.
14	
15	We state four assumptions maintained throughout.
16	%
17	\begin{itemize}
18	\item[\textbf{(A1)}] \textit{Conditional independence:} misclassification depends only on the true label $Z$ and subgroup $S$, not on potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1)$.
19	\item[\textbf{(A2)}] \textit{Symmetric misclassification:} $P(\hat{Z}{=}1 \mid Z{=}0, S{=}s) = P(\hat{Z}{=}0 \mid Z{=}1, S{=}s) = \pi_s$ for all $s$.
20	\item[\textbf{(A3)}] \textit{Balanced effect modifier:} $P(Z{=}0) = P(Z{=}1) = 0.5$. This simplifies the exposition; we discuss relaxation below.
21	\item[\textbf{(A4)}] \textit{Non-degeneracy:} $\pi_s \neq 0.5$ for all $s$, ensuring each $C_s$ is invertible.
22	\end{itemize}
23	
24	Under (A2)--(A3), the Bayesian mixing matrix $M_s$ (entries $M_s[\hat{z}, z] = P(Z{=}z \mid \hat{Z}{=}\hat{z}, S{=}s)$) coincides with $C_s$.
25	The global mixing matrix is $M_{\text{global}} = \sum_s w_s M_s$.
26	
27	\begin{theorem}[Bias Decomposition Identity]
28	\label{thm:bias_identity}
29	Under \textnormal{(A1)--(A4)}, the bias of global correction in subgroup $s$ at effect-modifier level $z$ is
30	\begin{align}
31	\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}(z{=}0, s) &= +\frac{\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau}{1 - 2\bar{\pi}}, \label{eq:bias_z0} \\
32	\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}(z{=}1, s) &= -\frac{\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau}{1 - 2\bar{\pi}}, \label{eq:bias_z1}
33	\end{align}
34	where $\delta_s = \pi_s - \bar{\pi}$ is the subgroup deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau = \tau(1) - \tau(0)$ is the CATE heterogeneity.
35	\end{theorem}
36	
37	Equations~\eqref{eq:bias_z0}--\eqref{eq:bias_z1} constitute an exact identity at the population level, not a bound.
38	The bias factors into three interpretable components: $\delta_s$ captures how much subgroup $s$ deviates from the average misclassification rate, $\Delta\tau$ captures treatment effect heterogeneity across levels of $Z$, and $1/(1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ is an amplification factor from matrix inversion.
39	Bias vanishes when either source of variation is absent ($\delta_s = 0$ or $\Delta\tau = 0$), and arises only through their interaction.
40	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} implies that global correction trades one source of confounding for another: it removes attenuation from label noise but introduces a new bias from error-rate heterogeneity.
41	
42	\paragraph{Proof sketch.}
43	Global correction applies $M_{\text{global}}^{-1}$ to the subgroup-specific observed CATE $\tau_{\text{obs}}(\cdot, s) = M_s \cdot \tau_{\text{true}}$, yielding bias $(M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s - I) \cdot \tau_{\text{true}}$.
44	Direct computation shows $M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s - I = \frac{\delta_s}{1-2\bar{\pi}} \bigl[\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{smallmatrix}\bigr]$.
45	Applying this matrix to $[\tau(0),\, \tau(1)]^\top$ produces the product form.
46	The full derivation appears in Appendix~\ref{app:derivation}.
47	
48	The identity extends to $K > 2$ subgroups with $J$ effect-modifier levels; the multi-class bias retains the same product structure with modified amplification terms (Corollary~\ref{cor:multiclass} in Appendix~\ref{app:multiclass}).
49	
50	Assumption~(A3) ensures $M_s = C_s$; when $P(Z{=}1) \neq 0.5$, the mixing matrices acquire asymmetric entries, but the product structure persists with modified coefficients (Appendix~\ref{app:derivation}).
51	Empirical verification (Section~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}) yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.974$ for $K{=}4$; the residual variance reflects finite-sample Monte Carlo noise, not model misspecification.
52	
53	\paragraph{Finite-sample remainder.}
54	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is an exact population identity.
55	In practice, confusion matrices are estimated from $n_{\text{expert}}$ expert labels, introducing an estimation error $\hat{C}_s = C_s + E_s$ where $\|E_s\| = O_p(n_{\text{expert}}^{-1/2})$.
56	The resulting remainder term in the corrected CATE is $R_n = O_p(n_{\text{expert}}^{-1/2} \cdot \kappa(C_s))$, where $\kappa(C_s)$ is the condition number of the subgroup confusion matrix.
57	This dependence on both sample size and matrix conditioning motivates the singularity guard ($\kappa > 100 \to$ fallback) described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
58	
59	\begin{proposition}[Debiasing Can Increase Bias]
60	\label{prop:debiasing_hurts}
61	Under \textnormal{(A1)--(A4)}, global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator ($|\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}| > |\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{naive}}|$) in subgroup $s$ if and only if
62	\begin{equation}
63	\frac{|\delta_s|}{(1 - 2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s} > 1.
64	\label{eq:hurts_condition}
65	\end{equation}
66	\end{proposition}
67	
68	Equation~\eqref{eq:hurts_condition} partitions subgroups into two regimes.
69	For high-error subgroups ($\pi_s > \bar{\pi}$), the condition reduces to $\pi_s > 0.5$, which is excluded by~(A4); global correction always reduces bias in these subgroups.
70	For low-error subgroups ($\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$), the condition holds whenever $\pi_s < \bar{\pi} / (2(1 - \bar{\pi}))$.
71	This threshold is easily satisfied in practice: when $\bar{\pi} = 0.15$, any subgroup with $\pi_s < 0.088$ experiences increased bias from global correction.
72	The mechanism is that global correction inverts the pooled confusion matrix, applying a correction calibrated for the average error rate; high-error subgroups are under-corrected (bias reduced but not eliminated), while low-error subgroups are over-corrected (the correction overshoots and reverses the sign of bias).
73	For subgroups with near-zero misclassification ($\pi_s \approx 0$), the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet global correction creates substantial bias where none existed.
74	This is the most consequential implication of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}: debiasing can be worse than doing nothing.
75	
76	In our experiments (Section~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}), global correction increases bias in 50\% of parameter configurations (260 of 520, excluding cases where $\Delta_c{=}0$).
77	With the difference-in-means estimator, maximum amplification reaches $2.86\times$ for $K{=}2$ and $2.41\times$ for $K{=}4$; the mechanism operates across estimator types, with nonlinear estimators amplifying the effect further (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}).
78	Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification across the full $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ parameter grid.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We identified an exact bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) showing that global confusion-matrix correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$, the product of misclassification heterogeneity and CATE heterogeneity.
This is not a bound but an exact population-level result, and it reveals that standard debiasing worsens subgroup CATE estimates in 50\% of experimental configurations.
EC-HTE addresses this through hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified correction combined with CausalForestDML (Section~\ref{sec:method}), with a computable diagnostic (AUC $= 0.83$) that identifies when stratified correction is warranted (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}).
Composition with PPCI handles dual covariate/outcome error, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007.

The recommended workflow is straightforward: compute $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ from a modest pilot sample (we use $n_{\text{expert}} = 50$ in our experiments); if the product is large for any subgroup, apply EC-HTE with $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$ ($K{=}2$) or $\geq 1{,}000$ ($K{=}4$); if uniformly small, global correction suffices.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional, not universal.
When error heterogeneity is low, the variance cost of per-subgroup estimation outweighs the bias reduction, and global correction remains the appropriate choice.
This conditionality is a feature of the framework: the diagnostic tells practitioners when to incur the cost of stratified correction and when not to.

Our validation uses symmetric misclassification and known subgroup structure.
Extending the bias decomposition identity to asymmetric confusion matrices, continuous or latent subgroup discovery, and online settings with streaming annotations are natural next steps.
As LLM annotation pipelines scale across the social sciences, the interaction between measurement error heterogeneity and causal effect heterogeneity will grow more consequential; the broader landscape of error-heterogeneity interactions in automated causal inference remains open.

[Director 指令] [Patch] 三个新实验结果整合进论文（Appendix 为主，主文少量引用）

实验已全部完成，需要整合 exp-004、exp-008、exp-010 的结果。以下是整合方案：

---

**1. Appendix 新增：Real-Data Case Study (exp-004)**

在 appendix.tex 新增一个 section "Real-Data Case Study: Hate Speech Detection"。

内容要点：
- UC Berkeley Measuring Hate Speech corpus, 2496 comments, GPT-4.1 标注 dehumanization
- 4 text-feature subgroups (platform × text_length), n=624 each
- **Δπ = 0.117**：真实数据证实 LLM 误分类异质性存在
- CATE 校正结果 **mixed**：EC-HTE |bias| > Global > Naive。原因：全局 FNR=53%，confusion matrix 条件数差，逆矩阵放大噪声
- 框架：**motivational**（问题存在性验证），不是 demonstrative（方法优越性验证）
- "This case study confirms that subgroup-varying misclassification rates are not an artifact of synthetic design but arise naturally in real NLP annotation tasks. The high baseline FNR (53%) illustrates a boundary condition: when overall misclassification is extreme, confusion matrix inversion amplifies noise regardless of stratification strategy."

数据来自 `artifacts/exp-004/`。

---

**2. Appendix 新增：Multi-LLM Consistency (exp-008)**

在 appendix.tex 新增一个 section "Cross-Model Consistency"。

内容要点：
- 6 个 OpenAI 模型 (GPT-3.5-turbo → GPT-5.4)，TweetEval sentiment 500 条
- Table: 6 模型 × effective Δπ (排除 n<10 子群)
  - gpt-3.5: 0.198, gpt-4-turbo: 0.149, gpt-4o-mini: 0.136, gpt-5.4: 0.114, gpt-4.1: 0.098, gpt-4o: 0.080
- **全部 > 0.05**
- 5/6 模型最差子群 = True_medium (has_hashtag + medium text)
- "Heterogeneous misclassification persists across model generations and scales within the OpenAI family, from GPT-3.5 to GPT-5.4. Newer models reduce absolute error rates but do not eliminate subgroup heterogeneity."
- Limitations footnote: "tested with a single API provider; cross-provider validation is left to future work"

数据来自 `artifacts/exp-008/`。

---

**3. Appendix 新增：Robustness to Subgroup Misspecification (exp-010)**

在 appendix.tex 新增一个 section "Robustness to Subgroup Misspecification"。

内容要点：
- 4 noise levels (0/10/25/50%) × K=2,4 × 100 MC
- Table: coverage across noise levels（核心指标）
  - EC-HTE coverage ≥ 0.945 across all configs
  - Naive coverage 0.875-0.919 (systematically below 95%)
  - Global coverage 0.925-0.953
- K=2 p_flip=0.50: EC-HTE statistically indistinguishable from global
- K=4 p_flip=0.50: coverage converges but RMSE retains small residual gap (p<0.01)
- "EC-HTE maintains near-nominal CI coverage even under severe subgroup misspecification (50% noise), confirming that hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage provides a built-in safety mechanism."

数据来自 `artifacts/exp-010/`。

---

**4. 主文引用（最小改动）**

在 experiments.tex 的适当位置加 1-2 句引用新 Appendix sections：
- "Real-data validation on hate speech detection confirms Δπ = 0.117 across text-feature subgroups (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech})."
- "The heterogeneity pattern persists across six OpenAI models spanning three generations (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm})."
- "EC-HTE maintains ≥94.5% coverage under up to 50% subgroup misspecification noise (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness})."

---

**注意**：主文 8 页限制不能超。新内容全在 Appendix。编译确认后不提交审稿。

226

234	| Other | 17.3% | 15.4% | 21.1% | 22.2% | 24.0% |
235	| White | 16.9% | 19.2% | 18.9% | 23.0% | 21.9% |
236	
237	Black annotators assign more extreme dehumanization scores (26.9% at level 4 vs 21.9% for White). This differential perception is a source of LLM misclassification heterogeneity — if an LLM's dehumanization assessment aligns more with the White majority, it will systematically under-classify dehumanization as perceived by Black annotators.

282	
283	---
284	
285	## 5. Pattern Consistency Feasibility
286	
287	### Can we demonstrate "global correction vs EC-HTE produces qualitatively different CATE distributions"?
288	
289	**Yes, Scheme A is well-suited.** The argument:
290	
291	1. **LLM as Z annotator**: An LLM classifies each comment's dehumanization level (Z) based on text alone. The LLM cannot observe annotator demographics. Due to training data composition (majority White perspectives), the LLM's dehumanization assessment likely correlates more with White annotators' perception.
292	
293	2. **Subgroup-specific LLM error**: For Black-targeted hate speech, Black annotators perceive significantly more dehumanization (26.9% at level 4) than White annotators (21.9%). An LLM trained predominantly on majority-perspective data would under-classify dehumanization from the Black annotator perspective. This is a **subgroup-specific misclassification pattern** — the LLM error rate on Z differs by S.
294	
295	3. **Global correction failure**: A global correction (single miscalibration function applied uniformly) would adjust Z based on the population-average error. This population average is dominated by White annotators (80% of data). Applying this correction to Black annotators' CATE estimates would *over-correct* in the wrong direction — spreading the majority-group bias to the minority group.
296	
297	4. **EC-HTE advantage**: EC-HTE estimates subgroup-specific correction functions. For Black annotators, EC-HTE would learn that LLM under-classifies dehumanization relative to their perception, and correct accordingly. For White annotators, the correction would be minimal. This produces qualitatively different CATE distributions:
298	   - Global correction: uniform shift across S → attenuates true heterogeneity
299	   - EC-HTE: heterogeneous correction → preserves or amplifies cross-group differences
300	
301	5. **Domain knowledge alignment**: The pattern is consistent with hate speech literature — racialized groups perceive hate speech targeting their group more severely, and this differential perception is exactly what an LLM trained on majority-perspective data would miss.
302	
303	### What we don't need
304	
305	- No ground truth CATE required — we show method difference, not accuracy
306	- No RCT — the observational T (target_race_black) has clear temporal/causal interpretation: the text either targets Black people or it doesn't, and this is determined before annotation
307	
308	### Potential concerns
309	
310	1. **`hate_speech_score` is per-comment**: Since the Rasch score is constant per comment, it cannot serve as Y if we want to study annotator-level heterogeneity. **Use ordinal labels (hatespeech, dehumanize) as Y instead** — they vary per annotation.
311	
312	2. **Annotations per comment are thin**: Median 2 annotations per comment. For CATE estimation, this limits within-comment comparison but is fine for across-comment estimation with covariates.
313	
314	3. **Confounding**: Comments targeting Black people come disproportionately from platform 1 (47.6% vs 28.7% for non-Black-targeted). Platform may confound T→Y. Can control by including platform as covariate.
315	
316	4. **Multi-label targets**: Some comments target multiple groups (e.g., target_race_black AND target_gender_women). These should be handled carefully — either exclude multi-target comments or include as covariates.
317	
318	---
319	
320	## 6. Recommended Final Mapping
321	
322	### Primary: Scheme A
323	
324	| Component | Variable | Operationalization |
325	|-----------|----------|--------------------|
326	| **T** | `target_race_black` | Binary (True/False) |
327	| **Y** | `hatespeech` ordinal | Per-annotation, 3-level (0=not hate, 1=ambiguous, 2=hate) |
328	| **Z** | Dehumanization level | LLM classifies text → binary (high/low), compare to human `dehumanize` |
329	| **S** | Annotator race | White / Black / Other (from one-hot flags) |
330	| **Covariates** | Platform, text length, other target flags | Control for confounding |
331	
332	### Rationale
333	
334	- **Largest treatment group** among target demographics (22,899 annotations)
335	- **Clear LLM misclassification heterogeneity** story (majority-perspective bias in dehumanization assessment)
336	- **Cell sizes ≥ 743** across all T×Z×S combinations
337	- **Domain-relevant**: hate speech against Black people is well-studied, making domain-knowledge-based evaluation credible
338	- **Observable Z×S interaction** in CATE estimates: the direction of treatment effect heterogeneity flips between low-Z and high-Z for Black vs White annotators
339	
340	### Secondary: Scheme C (Muslim-targeted × ideology)
341	
342	Use as robustness check — different T (religion instead of race) and different S (ideology instead of race), providing independent evidence.
343	
344	### Not recommended: Scheme B
345	
346	The gender-targeted scheme shows insufficient T main effect and negligible T×S interaction, making it a poor candidate for demonstrating EC-HTE vs. global correction divergence.
347

| **T** (treatment) | `target_religion_muslim` | Binary: does the comment target Muslims? |
| **Y** (outcome) | `hate_speech_score` | Per-comment continuous Rasch score |
| **Z** (effect modifier) | `violence` binarized (≥1 vs 0) | LLM-annotated violence level |
| **S** (subgroup) | Annotator ideology (Liberal vs Conservative) | From `annotator_ideology` |

**Cell sizes (T × Z × S, liberal/conservative only)**:

| T | Z (violence_any) | Conservative | Liberal |
|---|-------------------|-------------|---------|
| 0 | 0 | 16,683 | 34,031 |
| 0 | 1 | 15,481 | 32,021 |
| 1 | 0 | 1,391 | 2,998 |
| 1 | 1 | 1,718 | 4,039 |

**Min cell = 1,391 — sufficient.**

Notable T×S interaction for Muslim-targeted content: conservative annotators rate Muslim-targeted comments slightly more negatively (hate_speech_score mean -0.61) while liberal annotators rate them less negatively (-0.52). The gap is modest but the direction is meaningful for the application.

---

## 5. Pattern Consistency Feasibility

### Can we demonstrate "global correction vs EC-HTE produces qualitatively different CATE distributions"?

**Yes, Scheme A is well-suited.** The argument:

1. **LLM as Z annotator**: An LLM classifies each comment's dehumanization level (Z) based on text alone. The LLM cannot observe annotator demographics. Due to training data composition (majority White perspectives), the LLM's dehumanization assessment likely correlates more with White annotators' perception.

2. **Subgroup-specific LLM error**: For Black-targeted hate speech, Black annotators perceive significantly more dehumanization (26.9% at level 4) than White annotators (21.9%). An LLM trained predominantly on majority-perspective data would under-classify dehumanization from the Black annotator perspective. This is a **subgroup-specific misclassification pattern** — the LLM error rate on Z differs by S.

3. **Global correction failure**: A global correction (single miscalibration function applied uniformly) would adjust Z based on the population-average error. This population average is dominated by White annotators (80% of data). Applying this correction to Black annotators' CATE estimates would *over-correct* in the wrong direction — spreading the majority-group bias to the minority group.

4. **EC-HTE advantage**: EC-HTE estimates subgroup-specific correction functions. For Black annotators, EC-HTE would learn that LLM under-classifies dehumanization relative to their perception, and correct accordingly. For White annotators, the correction would be minimal. This produces qualitatively different CATE distributions:
   - Global correction: uniform shift across S → attenuates true heterogeneity
   - EC-HTE: heterogeneous correction → preserves or amplifies cross-group differences

5. **Domain knowledge alignment**: The pattern is consistent with hate speech literature — racialized groups perceive hate speech targeting their group more severely, and this differential perception is exactly what an LLM trained on majority-perspective data would miss.

### What we don't need

- No ground truth CATE required — we show method difference, not accuracy
- No RCT — the observational T (target_race_black) has clear temporal/causal interpretation: the text either targets Black people or it doesn't, and this is determined before annotation

### Potential concerns

1. **`hate_speech_score` is per-comment**: Since the Rasch score is constant per comment, it cannot serve as Y if we want to study annotator-level heterogeneity. **Use ordinal labels (hatespeech, dehumanize) as Y instead** — they vary per annotation.

2. **Annotations per comment are thin**: Median 2 annotations per comment. For CATE estimation, this limits within-comment comparison but is fine for across-comment estimation with covariates.

3. **Confounding**: Comments targeting Black people come disproportionately from platform 1 (47.6% vs 28.7% for non-Black-targeted). Platform may confound T→Y. Can control by including platform as covariate.

4. **Multi-label targets**: Some comments target multiple groups (e.g., target_race_black AND target_gender_women). These should be handled carefully — either exclude multi-target comments or include as covariates.

---

## 6. Recommended Final Mapping

### Primary: Scheme A

| Component | Variable | Operationalization |
|-----------|----------|--------------------|
| **T** | `target_race_black` | Binary (True/False) |
| **Y** | `hatespeech` ordinal | Per-annotation, 3-level (0=not hate, 1=ambiguous, 2=hate) |
| **Z** | Dehumanization level | LLM classifies text → binary (high/low), compare to human `dehumanize` |
| **S** | Annotator race | White / Black / Other (from one-hot flags) |
| **Covariates** | Platform, text length, other target flags | Control for confounding |

### Rationale

- **Largest treatment group** among target demographics (22,899 annotations)
- **Clear LLM misclassification heterogeneity** story (majority-perspective bias in dehumanization assessment)
- **Cell sizes ≥ 743** across all T×Z×S combinations
- **Domain-relevant**: hate speech against Black people is well-studied, making domain-knowledge-based evaluation credible
- **Observable Z×S interaction** in CATE estimates: the direction of treatment effect heterogeneity flips between low-Z and high-Z for Black vs White annotators

### Secondary: Scheme C (Muslim-targeted × ideology)

Use as robustness check — different T (religion instead of race) and different S (ideology instead of race), providing independent evidence.

### Not recommended: Scheme B

The gender-targeted scheme shows insufficient T main effect and negligible T×S interaction, making it a poor candidate for demonstrating EC-HTE vs. global correction divergence.

225	### Key Findings

229	   successfully removes misclassification contamination even with noisy subgroups.
230	
231	2. **RMSE shows bias-variance tradeoff**: Corrected methods have slightly higher
232	   RMSE than naive because matrix inversion amplifies CM estimation noise. The
233	   RMSE gap is small (<10%) and stable across noise levels.
234

236	   below nominal 95%). MLE/HB achieve 95-96% across all noise levels. For valid

243	   to global correction (subgroup structure is destroyed), confirming HB's
244	   built-in safeguard via shrinkage.
245	
246	### Paper Implications

249	
250	- EC-HTE correction does not catastrophically fail under subgroup misspecification.
251	- The primary benefit of EC-HTE is **inferential validity** (correct coverage),
252	  not point estimation accuracy (RMSE).
253	- HB's partial pooling provides a natural safeguard: as subgroup signal degrades,
254	  the method automatically shrinks toward the global estimate.
255	- Even at 50% subgroup noise, HB-based EC-HTE produces CIs with near-nominal
256	  coverage, while naive CIs systematically under-cover.
257	- Recommendation: report both RMSE and coverage; the coverage advantage is
258	  the strongest argument for EC-HTE under noisy subgroup definitions.

The per-z-level results reveal the core tradeoff:

- **Naive**: Has substantial systematic bias (z0: +0.04, z1: -0.05) due to

- **Corrected methods**: Successfully eliminate systematic bias (mean bias near 0)
  but increase variance through mixing-matrix inversion. RMSE is comparable or
  slightly higher than naive.
- **Coverage**: The critical differentiator. Naive achieves only ~87-92% coverage
  (below nominal 95%) because CIs don't account for misclassification bias.
  MLE/HB achieve ~95-96% (near nominal). Global is intermediate at ~93-95%.
- **Implication**: For valid statistical inference (hypothesis tests, CIs),
  the corrected methods are essential despite similar RMSE.

| 0.50 | 0.1107 | 0.1156 | 0.1158 | -4.5% | -4.7% | +0.2% |

## HB vs MLE Under Noise

HB's partial pooling acts as a regularizer: as subgroup labels become noisy,
EB learns a larger concentration parameter, shrinking per-subgroup CMs toward
the global mean.

### K=2

| p_flip | MLE RMSE | HB RMSE | HB Improvement |
|--------|----------|---------|----------------|
| 0.00 | 0.0897 | 0.0893 | +0.4% |
| 0.10 | 0.0882 | 0.0880 | +0.3% |
| 0.25 | 0.0814 | 0.0813 | +0.2% |
| 0.50 | 0.0799 | 0.0799 | +0.1% |

### K=4

| p_flip | MLE RMSE | HB RMSE | HB Improvement |
|--------|----------|---------|----------------|
| 0.00 | 0.1306 | 0.1294 | +0.9% |
| 0.10 | 0.1228 | 0.1221 | +0.6% |
| 0.25 | 0.1161 | 0.1157 | +0.4% |
| 0.50 | 0.1158 | 0.1156 | +0.2% |

## Coverage Analysis

### K=2

| p_flip | Naive | Global | MLE | HB |
|--------|-------|--------|-----|-----|
| 0.00 | 0.875 | 0.925 | 0.958 | 0.958 |
| 0.10 | 0.877 | 0.935 | 0.948 | 0.948 |
| 0.25 | 0.890 | 0.932 | 0.953 | 0.950 |
| 0.50 | 0.897 | 0.945 | 0.945 | 0.945 |

### K=4

| p_flip | Naive | Global | MLE | HB |
|--------|-------|--------|-----|-----|
| 0.00 | 0.904 | 0.930 | 0.956 | 0.956 |
| 0.10 | 0.916 | 0.953 | 0.958 | 0.958 |
| 0.25 | 0.909 | 0.948 | 0.960 | 0.960 |
| 0.50 | 0.919 | 0.944 | 0.945 | 0.946 |

## Conclusions

### Key Findings

1. **Bias elimination is robust to noise**: All corrected methods (global, MLE, HB)
   maintain near-zero systematic bias across all noise levels. The correction
   successfully removes misclassification contamination even with noisy subgroups.

2. **RMSE shows bias-variance tradeoff**: Corrected methods have slightly higher
   RMSE than naive because matrix inversion amplifies CM estimation noise. The
   RMSE gap is small (<10%) and stable across noise levels.

3. **Coverage is the decisive metric**: Naive coverage is 87-92% (systematically
   below nominal 95%). MLE/HB achieve 95-96% across all noise levels. For valid
   inference, correction is essential regardless of RMSE.

4. **HB consistently outperforms MLE**: HB has lower RMSE than MLE at every
   noise level and K value, confirming partial pooling helps.

5. **Graceful convergence at high noise**: At p_flip=0.50, MLE and HB converge
   to global correction (subgroup structure is destroyed), confirming HB's
   built-in safeguard via shrinkage.

### Paper Implications

For Reviewer Concern #4 (subgroup definition sensitivity):

- EC-HTE correction does not catastrophically fail under subgroup misspecification.
- The primary benefit of EC-HTE is **inferential validity** (correct coverage),
  not point estimation accuracy (RMSE).
- HB's partial pooling provides a natural safeguard: as subgroup signal degrades,
  the method automatically shrinks toward the global estimate.
- Even at 50% subgroup noise, HB-based EC-HTE produces CIs with near-nominal
  coverage, while naive CIs systematically under-cover.
- Recommendation: report both RMSE and coverage; the coverage advantage is
  the strongest argument for EC-HTE under noisy subgroup definitions.

\section{Real-Data Case Study: Hate Speech Detection}
\label{app:hatespeech}

We apply EC-HTE to the UC Berkeley Measuring Hate Speech corpus~\cite{kennedy2020constructing}, annotating 2{,}496 comments for dehumanization using GPT-4.1.
Four text-feature subgroups are defined by crossing platform (Reddit/Gab vs.\ Twitter/YouTube) and text length (above/below median), yielding balanced groups ($n \approx 624$ each).
Per-subgroup misclassification rates range from 0.266 to 0.383, confirming heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi = 0.117$) in a real annotation setting.

CATE correction results are mixed: EC-HTE does not improve over global correction, and both corrected estimators produce wider confidence intervals than the naive baseline.
The underlying cause is a global FNR of 53\%, which renders the confusion matrices near-singular (condition numbers $> 50$).
Under such extreme baseline error, matrix inversion amplifies noise regardless of stratification strategy.
This case study confirms that subgroup-varying misclassification rates are not an artifact of synthetic design but arise naturally in real NLP annotation tasks.
The high baseline FNR illustrates a boundary condition: when overall misclassification is extreme, EC-HTE's bias reduction is overwhelmed by variance from near-singular inversion, and practitioners should prioritize improving annotation quality before applying correction.

\section{Cross-Model Consistency}
\label{app:multilm}

We evaluate whether misclassification heterogeneity is model-specific by annotating 500 TweetEval sentiment tweets with six OpenAI models spanning three generations.
Small subgroups ($n < 10$) are excluded; effective $\Delta\pi$ is computed over the four retained text-feature subgroups.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Effective misclassification heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi$) across six OpenAI models on TweetEval sentiment (500 tweets, 4 subgroups with $n \geq 10$).}
\label{tab:multilm}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Model & Effective $\Delta\pi$ & $> 0.05$? \\
\midrule
GPT-3.5-Turbo & 0.198 & \checkmark \\
GPT-4-Turbo & 0.149 & \checkmark \\
GPT-4o-mini & 0.136 & \checkmark \\
GPT-5.4 & 0.114 & \checkmark \\
GPT-4.1 & 0.098 & \checkmark \\
GPT-4o & 0.080 & \checkmark \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All six models exhibit $\Delta\pi > 0.05$ (Table~\ref{tab:multilm}), and 5 of 6 share the same worst subgroup (\texttt{True\_medium}: tweets with hashtags and medium text length).
Spearman rank correlations of per-subgroup error rates between model pairs range from $\rho = 0.80$ to $1.00$, indicating that the subgroup error structure is consistent across architectures.
Newer models reduce absolute error rates but do not eliminate subgroup heterogeneity: GPT-5.4 achieves $\Delta\pi = 0.114$ compared to GPT-3.5-Turbo's $0.198$.
These results were obtained with a single API provider; cross-provider validation is left to future work.

\section{Robustness to Subgroup Misspecification}
\label{app:robustness}

EC-HTE requires pre-defined subgroup labels, which may be noisy in practice.
We test robustness by randomly flipping each observation's subgroup assignment with probability $p_{\text{flip}} \in \{0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50\}$, across $K \in \{2, 4\}$ (extreme regime, $n_{\text{expert}} = 500$, $\Delta\tau = 0.3$, 100 MC runs).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{95\% CI coverage under subgroup misspecification noise. EC-HTE maintains near-nominal coverage across all noise levels.}
\label{tab:robustness}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{4}{c}{$p_{\text{flip}}$} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-5}
Method & 0.00 & 0.10 & 0.25 & 0.50 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{5}{l}{\textit{$K{=}2$, extreme}} \\
\quad Naive & 0.875 & 0.877 & 0.890 & 0.897 \\
\quad Global & 0.925 & 0.935 & 0.932 & 0.945 \\
\quad HB EC-HTE & 0.958 & 0.948 & 0.950 & 0.945 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{5}{l}{\textit{$K{=}4$, extreme}} \\
\quad Naive & 0.904 & 0.916 & 0.909 & 0.919 \\
\quad Global & 0.930 & 0.953 & 0.948 & 0.944 \\
\quad HB EC-HTE & 0.956 & 0.958 & 0.960 & 0.946 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

EC-HTE maintains coverage $\geq 0.945$ across all configurations (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}), while the naive estimator is systematically below nominal (0.875--0.919).
At $p_{\text{flip}} = 0.50$, subgroup structure is effectively destroyed; EC-HTE converges to global correction (coverage and RMSE within 0.1\%), confirming that hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage provides a built-in safety mechanism.
For $K{=}4$ at $p_{\text{flip}} = 0.50$, a small residual RMSE gap persists ($p < 0.01$), reflecting the variance cost of estimating four confusion matrices even when they carry no signal.

The high baseline FNR illustrates a boundary condition: when overall misclassification is extreme, EC-HTE's bias reduction is overwhelmed by variance from near-singular inversion, and practitioners should prioritize improving annotation quality before applying correction.

\section{Cross-Model Consistency}
\label{app:multilm}

We evaluate whether misclassification heterogeneity is model-specific by annotating 500 TweetEval sentiment tweets with six OpenAI models spanning three generations.
Small subgroups ($n < 10$) are excluded; effective $\Delta\pi$ is computed over the four retained text-feature subgroups.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Effective misclassification heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi$) across six OpenAI models on TweetEval sentiment (500 tweets, 4 subgroups with $n \geq 10$).}
\label{tab:multilm}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Model & Effective $\Delta\pi$ & $> 0.05$? \\
\midrule
GPT-3.5-Turbo & 0.198 & \checkmark \\
GPT-4-Turbo & 0.149 & \checkmark \\
GPT-4o-mini & 0.136 & \checkmark \\

\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All six models exhibit $\Delta\pi > 0.05$ (Table~\ref{tab:multilm}), and 5 of 6 share the same worst subgroup (\texttt{True\_medium}: tweets with hashtags and medium text length).
Spearman rank correlations of per-subgroup error rates between model pairs range from $\rho = 0.80$ to $1.00$, indicating that the subgroup error structure is consistent across architectures.
Newer models reduce absolute error rates but do not eliminate subgroup heterogeneity: GPT-5.4 achieves $\Delta\pi = 0.114$ compared to GPT-3.5-Turbo's $0.198$.
These results were obtained with a single API provider; cross-provider validation is left to future work.

\section{Robustness to Subgroup Misspecification}
\label{app:robustness}

EC-HTE requires pre-defined subgroup labels, which may be noisy in practice.
We test robustness by randomly flipping each observation's subgroup assignment with probability $p_{\text{flip}} \in \{0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50\}$, across $K \in \{2, 4\}$ (extreme regime, $n_{\text{expert}} = 500$, $\Delta\tau = 0.3$, 100 MC runs).

\label{tab:robustness}

\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{4}{c}{$p_{\text{flip}}$} \\

Method & 0.00 & 0.10 & 0.25 & 0.50 \\

EC-HTE maintains coverage $\geq 0.945$ across all configurations (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}), while the naive estimator is systematically below nominal (0.875--0.919).
At $p_{\text{flip}} = 0.50$, subgroup structure is effectively destroyed; EC-HTE converges to global correction (coverage and RMSE within 0.1\%), confirming that hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage provides a built-in safety mechanism.

We evaluate on synthetic and semi-synthetic data generating processes (DGPs); full specifications appear in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
The synthetic DGP generates $N{=}5{,}000$ observations from a randomized trial with $K \in \{2, 4\}$ subgroups, controlled CATE heterogeneity $\Delta\tau$, and subgroup-specific symmetric misclassification rates with heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$.
Expert labels ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{50, \ldots, 2000\}$) are a simple random sample with true $Z$ observed; each configuration is repeated for 100 Monte Carlo runs.
The semi-synthetic DGP samples $N{=}5{,}000$ tweets from TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, defining $K{=}4$ subgroups by crossing hashtag presence and text length (unbalanced: 39\%/38\%/12\%/11\%), with misclassification rates $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$ reflecting empirical evidence that text features degrade LLM accuracy~\cite{ashwin2025bias}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup MLE without pooling), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.

In the semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment, the pattern shifts.
Global correction achieves the lowest $|\text{bias}|$ (0.023) among non-oracle methods, while HB EC-HTE attains 0.027 with substantially higher RMSE (0.225 vs.\ 0.124).
This is consistent with moderate $\Delta\pi{=}0.20$ and the high-error subgroups (S2, S3) comprising only 23\% of data: the bias reduction from stratification is marginal while the variance cost of four per-subgroup confusion matrices is substantial.
HB EC-HTE does improve over stratified MLE (RMSE 0.225 vs.\ 0.248), confirming that partial pooling helps, but the improvement is insufficient to overcome the structural variance from unbalanced subgroup sizes.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, HB and MLE converge to within 5\% on all metrics.

\paragraph{CausalForest K-dependence.}
When the downstream estimator is a CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, the bias mechanism operates with amplified magnitude.
At $K{=}4$/extreme/$n{=}500$, EC-HTE Forest reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 (global) to 0.040, a 4.8$\times$ improvement with dramatically better coverage (0.91 vs.\ 0.58).
The debiasing-hurts phenomenon intensifies: global correction amplifies naive bias by up to 5.9$\times$ in the worst subgroup, because the forest's sensitivity to covariate noise magnifies the effect of label errors.
At $K{=}4$/$n{=}100$, EC-HTE Forest RMSE reaches 1.43 (3.5$\times$ naive), underscoring the budget guidelines in Section~\ref{sec:budget}.

10	We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup MLE without pooling), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
11	For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
12	Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.

14	\subsection{Bias Mechanism Verification}
15	\label{sec:bias_mechanism}
16	
17	The bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) predicts that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ at the subgroup level.
18	We verify this identity empirically across 520 configurations spanning $K \in \{2,4\}$, two misclassification regimes, and six expert budget levels.
19	Regressing observed subgroup bias on the predicted $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.974$ for $K{=}4$; the residual variance reflects MC sampling noise rather than model misspecification, since Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is an exact identity at the population level.
20	In 50\% of configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta_c{=}0$ rows where bias is zero by construction), global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator.
21	The damage concentrates in low-$\pi$ subgroups: among subgroups where $\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$, global correction increases bias in 84.6\% of cases.
22	Maximum observed amplification reaches 2.86$\times$ (K=2) and 2.41$\times$ (K=4) relative to the naive estimator.
23	Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ amplification surface across the parameter grid.

29	\label{fig:heatmap}
30	\end{figure*}
31

33	\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}
34	
35	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.

37	The advantage persists at $K{=}4$: EC-HTE achieves $|\text{bias}|{=}0.009$ versus 0.056 for global (6.2$\times$ reduction), though with a small RMSE penalty (0.127 vs.\ 0.125).
38	Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), global correction already achieves low bias (0.009), and EC-HTE provides negligible improvement (0.005) at the cost of slightly higher RMSE (0.075 vs.\ 0.074).
39	This illustrates the conditional nature of EC-HTE's advantage: when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification is not offset by bias reduction.
40	
41	In the semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment, the pattern shifts.
42	Global correction achieves the lowest $|\text{bias}|$ (0.023) among non-oracle methods, while HB EC-HTE attains 0.027 with substantially higher RMSE (0.225 vs.\ 0.124).

98	Using leave-one-out cross-validation at the subgroup level, a threshold classifier on $|\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau|$ achieves AUC = 0.83 for predicting whether global correction increases bias relative to the naive estimator.

\section{Experiments}

We evaluate on synthetic and semi-synthetic data generating processes (DGPs); full specifications appear in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
The synthetic DGP generates $N{=}5{,}000$ observations from a randomized trial with $K \in \{2, 4\}$ subgroups, controlled CATE heterogeneity $\Delta\tau$, and subgroup-specific symmetric misclassification rates with heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$.
Expert labels ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{50, \ldots, 2000\}$) are a simple random sample with true $Z$ observed; each configuration is repeated for 100 Monte Carlo runs.
The semi-synthetic DGP samples $N{=}5{,}000$ tweets from TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, defining $K{=}4$ subgroups by crossing hashtag presence and text length (unbalanced: 39\%/38\%/12\%/11\%), with misclassification rates $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$ reflecting empirical evidence that text features degrade LLM accuracy~\cite{ashwin2025bias}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup MLE without pooling), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.

\subsection{Bias Mechanism Verification}
\label{sec:bias_mechanism}

The bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) predicts that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ at the subgroup level.
We verify this identity empirically across 520 configurations spanning $K \in \{2,4\}$, two misclassification regimes, and six expert budget levels.
Regressing observed subgroup bias on the predicted $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.974$ for $K{=}4$; the residual variance reflects MC sampling noise rather than model misspecification, since Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is an exact identity at the population level.
In 50\% of configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta_c{=}0$ rows where bias is zero by construction), global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator.
The damage concentrates in low-$\pi$ subgroups: among subgroups where $\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$, global correction increases bias in 84.6\% of cases.
Maximum observed amplification reaches 2.86$\times$ (K=2) and 2.41$\times$ (K=4) relative to the naive estimator.
Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ amplification surface across the parameter grid.

\label{fig:heatmap}
\end{figure*}

\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
In the synthetic DGP with $K{=}2$ subgroups and extreme misclassification heterogeneity, HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 (global) to 0.011 (a 5.4$\times$ reduction) while maintaining nominal coverage (0.95) and comparable RMSE (0.093 vs.\ 0.099).
The advantage persists at $K{=}4$: EC-HTE achieves $|\text{bias}|{=}0.009$ versus 0.056 for global (6.2$\times$ reduction), though with a small RMSE penalty (0.127 vs.\ 0.125).
Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), global correction already achieves low bias (0.009), and EC-HTE provides negligible improvement (0.005) at the cost of slightly higher RMSE (0.075 vs.\ 0.074).
This illustrates the conditional nature of EC-HTE's advantage: when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification is not offset by bias reduction.

Global correction achieves the lowest $|\text{bias}|$ (0.023) among non-oracle methods, while HB EC-HTE attains 0.027 with substantially higher RMSE (0.225 vs.\ 0.124).
This is consistent with moderate $\Delta\pi{=}0.20$ and the high-error subgroups (S2, S3) comprising only 23\% of data: the bias reduction from stratification is marginal while the variance cost of four per-subgroup confusion matrices is substantial.
HB EC-HTE does improve over stratified MLE (RMSE 0.225 vs.\ 0.248), confirming that partial pooling helps, but the improvement is insufficient to overcome the structural variance from unbalanced subgroup sizes.

\label{sec:diagnostic}

As a practical corollary of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}, the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product provides a computable diagnostic for predicting when global correction will fail.
Using leave-one-out cross-validation at the subgroup level, a threshold classifier on $|\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau|$ achieves AUC = 0.83 for predicting whether global correction increases bias relative to the naive estimator.
The Pearson correlation between the signed product and the observed bias ratio is $r = 0.86$.
At the setting level (averaging across subgroups within a configuration), the diagnostic has AUC = 0.47, which is no better than random.
This asymmetry arises because global correction redistributes bias across subgroups (benefiting high-$\pi$ subgroups at the expense of low-$\pi$ ones) rather than increasing total bias uniformly.
In practice, the diagnostic enables researchers to identify vulnerable subgroups before committing to a correction strategy: if any subgroup has $\pi_s \ll \bar{\pi}$ and $\tau(z)$ varies across $z$-levels, global correction should be avoided.
Figure~\ref{fig:roc} (Appendix) shows the ROC curve and correlation scatter plot.

\subsection{Expert Budget Analysis}
\label{sec:budget}

The crossover point at which EC-HTE achieves lower RMSE than global correction is $n_{\text{expert}} = 250$ for $K{=}2$/extreme and $n_{\text{expert}} = 1000$ for $K{=}4$/extreme (Figure~\ref{fig:budget} in the Appendix).
Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), EC-HTE never achieves lower RMSE than global at any budget.
HB partial pooling improves over stratified MLE in 21 of 24 configurations, with the two estimators converging by $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$.

\subsection{PPCI Complementarity}
\label{sec:ppci}

EC-HTE corrects covariate misclassification but cannot address outcome-level error; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects outcome-level error but assumes correct covariates.
Under both error types simultaneously (DGP~C), EC-HTE+PPCI reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 ($z{=}0$), a $25\times$ improvement over EC-HTE alone (Table~\ref{tab:ppci} in the Appendix).
Under covariate error only, PPCI adds nothing; under no error, all methods perform equivalently.
The two corrections are complementary: EC-HTE handles covariate-side $M^{-1}$ inversion while PPCI handles residual outcome-level bias.
